title: What AI can and can't do for you

slides.h: What AI can and can't do for you
slides.p: Three minutes to know where Claude saves you time, and where you stay in charge.

slides.h: Think of a fast, well-read assistant for words
slides.p: Claude reads, writes, summarises, translates and sorts text very well. Anything your team does with emails, documents and messages is a candidate.

slides.h: Where it saves time this week
items: Replies to the questions you answer every day
Menus, product texts and posts in three languages
First drafts of quotes and proposals
Meeting notes turned into a to-do list

slides.h: What it can't do on its own
items: Know your prices, clients or stock unless you give them
Be right every time: it can sound sure and still be wrong
Decide for you: your judgement stays the last step

slides.h: Treat it like a new colleague's draft
slides.p: Read before you send. Check numbers, names, dates and anything you would be embarrassed to get wrong.
slides.ex: 40 supplier emails → a one-page summary of what's late, what changed and what needs an answer. You check the summary in 5 minutes instead of reading for an hour.

slides.p: Paste a few real emails you received this week and use this:
slides.prompt: Here are 5 emails I received this week. Group them by topic, tell me which ones need an answer today, and draft a short, friendly and professional reply for each.

slides.p: Claude drafts, sorts and translates; you check and decide. Next: how to ask well.
The quality of the answer depends on the quality of the request. Here is how to brief Claude like a good colleague.

slides.h: A good request has four parts
items: Context: who you are and who it's for
Task: what you want, exactly
Limits: length, tone, language
An example of what good looks like

slides.after: I run a family trattoria in Bologna. Write 3 menu descriptions (max 20 words each) for our tagliatelle al ragù, in Italian and English. Warm, not fancy. Here's one we like: “Our nonna's Sunday ragù, slow-cooked for six hours.”

slides.p: The first answer is a starting point. Say “shorter”, “more formal”, “give me three options” or “keep the second one and change the ending”. Two or three rounds usually get you there.

items: Paste the real material: the email, the price list, the notes
Ask it to ask you questions if something is missing
Say what to avoid, not only what you want

slides.p: Pick one text you write often and fill in the brackets:
slides.prompt: I run [your business] in [city]. Write [what] for [who], in [language], max [length]. The tone should be [tone]. Here is an example we like: [paste]. Before you start, ask me anything you need to know.

slides.p: Context, task, limits, example, then refine together. Next: give Claude your company's knowledge once.

title: Your company's knowledge, in one place

slides.h: Your company's knowledge, in one place
slides.p: Stop re-explaining your business in every chat.

slides.h: Projects: a room for each part of your work
slides.p: In Claude, a Project holds documents and instructions you set once. Every conversation inside it already knows them.

items: Price list, opening hours, policies
Your most frequent questions and good answers
Examples of texts in your tone of voice
Menu, catalogue or service descriptions

slides.ex: You answer as the team of Trattoria Da Giulia. Reply in the customer's language. Be warm and brief. Never confirm a booking yourself: suggest times and say we will confirm within the hour.

items: One project per area: customers, suppliers, marketing
Update the documents when prices or hours change
Keep private data out of it unless your plan and policy allow it

slides.p: Create a project called “Customer replies”, add your FAQ and price list, paste the instructions above, then test it with a real message:
slides.prompt: A customer wrote this: [paste]. Draft our reply using the project's information. Tell me if anything is missing from our documents.

slides.p: Set up your knowledge once, and every answer starts from your business. That's the base for everything that follows.
